From self-evident logical axioms — Heidegger followed the Cartesian tradition in seeking indubitable starting points for a system of knowledge.
From inner introspection — the philosopher locates a stream of conscious states and then asks what their existence implies about the outside world.
From experimental data — Heidegger thought philosophy after Husserl had to anchor itself in the natural sciences to avoid speculative drift over time.
context: Being and Time §§15–18. The 'ready-to-hand' (zuhanden) hammer disappearing into hammering comes before the 'present-at-hand' object of theory.

question: Merleau-Ponty thought Descartes had left a riddle and pretended it was solved. A mind that thinks, a body that moves — no honest account of how the two are joined. Husserl's transcendental ego inherited the same problem. What did he put in the disembodied subject's place?
answer: The lived body — perception is something the body does, with the world taking shape around postures, reaches, and skills before any inner judgment forms.
choices: The lived body — perception is something the body does, with the world taking shape around postures, reaches, and skills before any inner judgment forms.
The transcendent God — the gap between inner mind and outer body is bridged by a divine agent who carries information across the divide each moment.
The pineal gland — a small organ at the brain's base where mental and physical events causally meet, just as Descartes himself had once proposed.
The neural network — the brain alone does the work, and what we call mind is simply a high-level description of certain physical events going on in it.
context: Phenomenology of Perception (1945). One of the most influential 20th-century alternatives to mind-body dualism — neither idealist nor materialist.

question: The later Wittgenstein imagined someone trying to name a private sensation 'S' — simply pointing at it inwardly each time it returns and marking the calendar. Why, on his argument in Investigations §§243–315, does the private language not work?
answer: There is no way to check whether the second 'S' really matches the first — without a public criterion, 'right' and 'seems right' collapse together.
choices: There is no way to check whether the second 'S' really matches the first — without a public criterion, 'right' and 'seems right' collapse together.
Private sensations do not exist as Cartesians imagined them; the mind is empty of qualia, and the supposed inner pointing has nothing to point at.
The diarist will simply forget after a few days; memory in adults is not reliable enough to ground a stable private vocabulary over time.
Language is a social product invented historically by communities; only words that arose in collective speech can be used meaningfully at all.
context: The private-language argument is one of the most disputed passages in 20th-century philosophy; Kripke read it as a paradox about following any rule.

question: Marx's theory of historical materialism predicts capitalism's collapse from internal contradictions — the falling rate of profit, the concentration of capital, the immiseration of workers. Mises and Hayek argued from the 1920s onward that something specific would block any planned successor system. What was their argument?
answer: Without market prices for capital goods, no planner can rationally allocate scarce resources — central planning cannot perform the calculation a price system performs.
choices: Without market prices for capital goods, no planner can rationally allocate scarce resources — central planning cannot perform the calculation a price system performs.
Without strong incentives, individual workers will not work hard enough to sustain output — moral exhortation alone fails to replace the threat of unemployment.
Without religious belief, citizens lose all motive for sacrifice — secular regimes cannot generate the loyalty older societies got from established churches.
Without ethnic homogeneity, large planned states fragment along nationalist lines — Marx had failed to anticipate the strength of national feeling.
context: Mises's 1920 essay 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth' and Hayek's 1945 'Use of Knowledge in Society' framed the central theoretical critique of planning.

question: Heidegger spent the first half of Being and Time on what he called the 'existential analytic of Dasein' — careful descriptions of how a human being already finds itself in the world: thrown, attuned, with others, moving toward death. The book's title points beyond all of that. What was Heidegger's ultimate purpose?
answer: To use Dasein's special way of being — the one entity for whom its own being is in question — as a route into the still-unanswered meaning of being itself.
choices: To use Dasein's special way of being — the one entity for whom its own being is in question — as a route into the still-unanswered meaning of being itself.
To replace academic philosophy with a kind of secular spiritual practice — Dasein-analysis was meant to help individuals live more authentically.
To ground a new German national philosophy in the soil of Black Forest peasant life — the politics of authenticity was the actual point of the book.
To prove the existence of an immortal soul — death was, in Heidegger's argument, the moment Dasein steps fully beyond the temporal world.
context: Being and Time was published unfinished — Part Two never appeared. The work as published is the preparation; the question of being itself was never delivered.

question: Russell once compared his theory of descriptions to a 'paradigm of philosophy.' The phrase puzzled later readers — what makes a piece of analysis a paradigm? Strawson in 1950 attacked the theory of descriptions head-on. What did Strawson argue Russell had gotten wrong?
answer: Sentences about nonexistent objects do not state false propositions; they presuppose what fails to hold, and a presupposition failure is not the same as falsity.
choices: Sentences about nonexistent objects do not state false propositions; they presuppose what fails to hold, and a presupposition failure is not the same as falsity.
Sentences about nonexistent objects refer to a special class of 'subsisting' entities, restoring the very ontology Russell had set out to eliminate from logic.
Sentences about nonexistent objects are simply meaningless, and Russell's elaborate analysis was answering a question that no real language ever asks.
Sentences about nonexistent objects can only be analyzed in modal logic, with reference securing itself across possible worlds rather than at the actual world.
context: Strawson, 'On Referring' (1950). The debate launched the field of pragmatics — the gap between what a sentence says and what its use presupposes.

question: Foucault distinguished what he called genealogy from older history. Older historians, on his picture, traced concepts and institutions back to their origins, seeking the true essence at the start. Foucault's genealogy works the opposite way. What does it do?
answer: It locates a concept inside the contingent struggles that formed it — showing that what looks natural is the residue of historical conflicts that could have gone differently.
choices: It locates a concept inside the contingent struggles that formed it — showing that what looks natural is the residue of historical conflicts that could have gone differently.
It locates a concept inside its purest classical formulation — showing that later thinkers have only diluted what an originating philosopher had said with clarity.
It locates a concept inside the economic base of the society that produced it — showing that ideas are reflections of material interests in the way Marx had said.
It locates a concept inside the unconscious mind of the thinkers who used it — showing that the surface meaning hides a Freudian wish those thinkers concealed.
context: 'Nietzsche, Genealogy, History' (1971). Foucault inherits the term from Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals and turns it against the search for hidden essences.

question: Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor confronts a silent Christ in 16th-century Seville. The Church, the Inquisitor explains, has fixed what Jesus left dangerously incomplete. Christ asked too much of ordinary people — freedom of conscience above bread, miracle, authority. What charge does the Inquisitor lay against Christ?
answer: That genuine freedom is a burden too heavy for most human beings — Christ should have given the world bread, miracle, and authority rather than the freedom to choose.
choices: That genuine freedom is a burden too heavy for most human beings — Christ should have given the world bread, miracle, and authority rather than the freedom to choose.
That genuine faith is impossible in any organized institution — Christ was right but the Church corrupted the message past saving within a few generations.
That genuine morality is incompatible with miracle — Christ was right in his ethics but the supernatural framing repelled the very people he sought to reach.
That genuine love is impossible across class divisions — Christ failed to address the material conditions that make the rich indifferent to the suffering of the poor.
context: The Brothers Karamazov, Book V (1880). Ivan tells the story to his brother Alyosha; Dostoevsky framed it as a thought experiment against any 'managed' religion.

question: Samkhya, one of the six orthodox Hindu schools, posited two eternal principles — purusa (pure consciousness) and prakriti (primal nature). Purusa never acts; prakriti acts without consciousness. The school used this to explain the experience of suffering. How?
answer: Suffering arises when purusa mistakes itself for the changing states of prakriti — liberation is not changing the world but seeing that consciousness was never the changing thing it had identified with.
choices: Suffering arises when purusa mistakes itself for the changing states of prakriti — liberation is not changing the world but seeing that consciousness was never the changing thing it had identified with.
Suffering arises when prakriti develops faster than purusa can absorb the changes — the school recommended slowing material activity through asceticism to let consciousness catch up.
Suffering arises when purusa and prakriti act on each other directly — the school taught a discipline that built a buffer between them so the interaction would calm down over time.
Suffering arises when prakriti is misperceived as conscious — the school's central practice was learning to see plants and animals as the unconscious matter they really were under the surface.
context: Samkhya is presented in the Samkhya Karika of Isvarakrsna (c. 4th century CE). It is dualist in a way unusual for Indian philosophy: not mind vs. matter exactly, but pure witness vs. unconscious natural process. Liberation (kaivalya) is the disentanglement of the witness from what it had falsely identified with — the seeing-through, not the changing. Yoga as a school took Samkhya's metaphysics and added theistic devotion plus an eightfold practice for cultivating the recognition.

question: Solomon Ibn Gabirol, eleventh-century poet and philosopher in Muslim Spain, wrote Fons Vitae — the Fountain of Life — entirely in Arabic. Latin Christians read it for centuries without knowing its author was Jewish. What metaphysical claim made the book so widely received?
answer: That every being below God is composed of matter and form — including the angels and rational souls — universal hylomorphism extending Aristotle's doctrine to all created intelligences.
choices: That every being below God is composed of matter and form — including the angels and rational souls — universal hylomorphism extending Aristotle's doctrine to all created intelligences.
That souls migrate from body to body across many lives — a doctrine of transmigration that Ibn Gabirol drew from Pythagorean sources and that the Latin scholastics accepted as authoritative.
That every being below God is purely spiritual in the angels and purely material in the bodies, with rational souls alone uniquely combining both natures in their singular composition.
That every being below God is created by emanation in necessary cascading stages — a Plotinian doctrine that Aquinas would later cite favorably against the creationist alternatives of his era.
context: Ibn Gabirol (c. 1021-1058), known in Latin as Avicebron or Avicebrol, was thought by Latin scholastics to be an Arab or even a Christian until Solomon Munk in 1846 identified Avicebron with the Hebrew poet Ibn Gabirol. The universal hylomorphism (matter even in spiritual substances) became standard Franciscan doctrine through Bonaventure and Scotus, while Aquinas and the Dominicans rejected it for angels. The case illustrates how medieval philosophical lineages crossed religious boundaries unawares.

question: Tertullian, the second-century North African Christian, asked one of the most famous rhetorical questions in patristic literature: 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?' Critics have read him as anti-philosophical. What was he actually arguing?
answer: That Christian doctrine has its own source in revelation and cannot be subordinated to Greek philosophy — not that reason is rejected, but that it cannot stand judge over what reason did not produce.
choices: That Christian doctrine has its own source in revelation and cannot be subordinated to Greek philosophy — not that reason is rejected, but that it cannot stand judge over what reason did not produce.
That all philosophy is sinful and must be entirely avoided by Christians — Tertullian's rigorism extended to a blanket prohibition on reading non-Christian authors of any kind whatsoever.
That faith and reason occupy completely separate domains — Tertullian anticipated by sixteen centuries the modern theory of non-overlapping magisteria that Stephen Jay Gould later named.
That Greek philosophy is morally inferior to Roman law — Tertullian wanted Christians to use juridical rather than philosophical categories in their theological reasoning across the board.
context: Tertullian's De Praescriptione Haereticorum 7 includes the famous question. The context is his complaint against gnostics who used Greek philosophical schemes to alter Christian teaching. His point is not that reasoning is bad — his own treatises argue carefully — but that Christian content has its own source and standards. His more notorious 'credo quia absurdum' formulation is a later misquotation; what he actually wrote (De Carne Christi 5) was 'certum est, quia impossibile' — and even that was a rhetorical move within an argument, not an irrationalist creed.

question: Alvin Plantinga in the 1970s defended the free will defense — the answer that an all-good, all-powerful God might still create a world containing evil if evil is the necessary cost of human freedom. He pressed one specific point against critics. What was it?
answer: It is logically possible that every world containing free beings also contains some evil — the defense need not establish probability, only consistency, to defeat the logical problem of evil.
choices: It is logically possible that every world containing free beings also contains some evil — the defense need not establish probability, only consistency, to defeat the logical problem of evil.
It is empirically established that worlds with free beings have more good than worlds without them — the defense rests on inductive comparison among the actual range of human societies.
It is morally evident that freedom is the highest good — the defense argues from the priority of freedom over comfort that any cost in suffering is automatically worth paying for it.
It is theologically required by scripture that humans be free — the defense draws its central premise from Christian revelation rather than from independent philosophical considerations.
context: Plantinga's God, Freedom, and Evil (1974) developed the free will defense against the logical problem of evil pressed by J.L. Mackie. Mackie had argued that no consistent set of propositions includes 'God is all-good,' 'God is omnipotent,' and 'evil exists.' Plantinga's reply added 'every world with free creatures contains some evil' as a logically possible proposition, which would make the set consistent. The defense is widely held to have shifted the burden — the live problem became the evidential problem (whether evil counts against theism as evidence), not the logical one.

question: William Paley in 1802 imagined finding a watch on a heath. He argued the watch implies a watchmaker; the world is far more complex; so the world implies a worldmaker. Darwin half a century later attacked the argument by removing one premise that Paley had needed. Which one?
answer: That the only known route to apparent design is intelligent design — natural selection showed that cumulative effects of variation and inheritance can generate complex adaptive structures without a designer.
choices: That the only known route to apparent design is intelligent design — natural selection showed that cumulative effects of variation and inheritance can generate complex adaptive structures without a designer.
That a designer must be intelligent and benevolent — Darwin allowed for a malevolent or incompetent designer responsible for the wasteful and cruel aspects of natural arrangements.
That biological complexity is greater than mechanical complexity — Darwin held that mechanical artifacts are actually more complex than organisms once both are properly analyzed.
That the analogy between organisms and machines holds — Darwin pointed out that organisms reproduce themselves and machines do not, breaking the analogy at its load-bearing point.
context: Paley's Natural Theology was the canonical English presentation of the design argument; it was on the Cambridge curriculum when Darwin studied there. The argument's force came partly from the absence of any rival explanation for apparent design. Darwin's Origin of Species (1859) supplied the rival: natural selection acting on heritable variation can produce the appearance of design across many generations without any guiding intelligence. The argument has since been refined (Behe's irreducible complexity, fine-tuning arguments at the cosmological level) but the original Paley version requires the no-rival-explanation premise.

question: Many Indigenous American philosophical traditions hold what scholars call a relational ontology — beings are constituted by their relations rather than by independent essences. How does this contrast with the dominant Western framework?
answer: Western metaphysics typically takes individual substances as primary and relations as features they happen to have; relational ontology takes relations as primary and the relata as features of the network.
choices: Western metaphysics typically takes individual substances as primary and relations as features they happen to have; relational ontology takes relations as primary and the relata as features of the network.
Western metaphysics typically takes ideas as primary and material things as copies; relational ontology takes material things as primary and ideas as patterns we recognize in our practices later.

Western metaphysics typically takes mind and matter as separate substances; relational ontology unifies them into one substance with two attributes, in close parallel to the position Spinoza defended.

Western metaphysics typically takes the universal as primary and the particular as instances; relational ontology reverses this priority, treating particulars as basic and universals as later abstractions.
context: Indigenous philosophers including Brian Burkhart, Dennis McPherson, Anne Waters, and Viola Cordova have developed relational ontology against the Aristotelian substance-and-attribute framework. The view has structural similarities to Whitehead's process philosophy and to some readings of Heidegger, but its sources are the actual practices of Indigenous communities — kinship systems that include land, animals, and ancestors as relatives in a literal not metaphorical sense. The Wabanaki, Diné, Lakota, and others have related but distinct articulations.

question: Henry Odera Oruka developed sage philosophy in Kenya from the 1970s onward. He conducted interviews with Luo elders identified by their communities as wise. What philosophical category did he defend with this work?
answer: Sages who think critically within a tradition rather than just transmitting it — individual African thinkers whose reflective work meets the standard of philosophy even without literacy or formal training.
choices: Sages who think critically within a tradition rather than just transmitting it — individual African thinkers whose reflective work meets the standard of philosophy even without literacy or formal training.
Folklorists who collect proverbs and stories that contain implicit philosophical wisdom — Oruka aimed to preserve the dying oral traditions of pre-colonial Africa from disappearing entirely.
Religious specialists whose ritual expertise carries metaphysical implications — Oruka studied them as a way of recovering an indigenous African theology that colonial missionaries had suppressed.
Political leaders who articulate the deepest values of their communities through their decisions — Oruka treated traditional authority itself as a form of practical philosophical work in action.
context: Oruka's Sage Philosophy: Indigenous Thinkers and Modern Debate on African Philosophy (1990) collected interviews with about a dozen Kenyan sages including Paul Mbuya Akoko, Stephen M'Mukindia Kithanje, and others. His category of philosophic sagacity — as distinguished from mere culture-philosophy — answered Hountondji's worry that African philosophy needed actual individual thinkers, not just collective traditions. The sages disagreed with each other and with received wisdom in ways Oruka thought met the philosophical threshold.

question: Kwame Nkrumah developed a political philosophy he called consciencism, set out in his 1964 book of that name. He argued that African society faced three competing intellectual currents and needed a synthesis. What were the three currents?
answer: Traditional African humanism, Euro-Christian inheritance from colonial education, and Islamic civilization from across the Sahara — each present in real African societies and requiring integration.
choices: Traditional African humanism, Euro-Christian inheritance from colonial education, and Islamic civilization from across the Sahara — each present in real African societies and requiring integration.
Capitalism imposed by colonizers, socialism imposed by Soviet allies, and the indigenous tribal economies of pre-colonial Africa — Nkrumah aimed to fuse the productive elements of each.

British common law inherited from colonization, French civil law from neighboring states, and customary law from traditional African legal systems — the synthesis would be a new African jurisprudence.
Western political liberalism, Marxist revolutionary theory, and traditional African monarchy — Nkrumah held that no system imported from outside could function without a continuity link to monarchy.
context: Nkrumah's Consciencism: Philosophy and Ideology for Decolonisation (1964) was written by Ghana's first president as an explicit philosophical framework for newly independent African nations. The three currents — pre-colonial African humanism, Christianity-via-Europe, and Islam — were each real intellectual presences that he held needed integration rather than dismissal of any one of them. The work has been criticized for its philosophical roughness and praised for the seriousness with which it took African intellectual agency.

question: Chalmers entertained a position called 'panpsychism' for one specific philosophical reason. What did he say recommended the strange-sounding view?
answer: It dissolves the hard problem: if experience is everywhere in some primitive form, no special story is needed for how brains generate what nothing else has.
choices: It dissolves the hard problem: if experience is everywhere in some primitive form, no special story is needed for how brains generate what nothing else has.
It avoids dualism: by giving mind a place in the physical, panpsychism keeps the world unified without leaving consciousness mysterious.
It fits ancient traditions: many premodern cultures saw mind in nature, and respect for that intuition recommends the position philosophically.
It explains paranormal reports: low-level mental phenomena would link minds across space, accounting for accounts that materialism cannot.
context: Chalmers's interest in panpsychism is structural, not mystical. The hard problem asks why brains alone generate experience. If experience is built into matter at the bottom — at some primitive 'proto-phenomenal' level — then brains do not need to *generate* it. They aggregate it. The 'combination problem' (how small experiences add up to big ones) is the cost.

question: Sider defends 'ontological realism' against the view that ontological questions are mere verbal disputes. What does Sider think such questions are about?
answer: The world's own joints — the basic categories nature would carve at, independent of human languages or interests in describing them.
choices: The world's own joints — the basic categories nature would carve at, independent of human languages or interests in describing them.
The pragmatic uses of language — which categories serve human purposes best, with no further fact about which the world prefers.
The conceptual confusions of philosophers — Sider thinks most metaphysics dissolves once careful analysis exposes the mistakes underlying it.
The history of philosophy — Sider treats ontological positions as products of their period rather than as candidates for present truth.
context: Sider's Writing the Book of the World (2011) argues that some categories — perhaps 'electron,' 'set,' 'cause' — pick out the world's structure more accurately than others — perhaps 'thing-Wednesday-that-fits-in-a-shoe.' The metaphysician's task is to find which categories are 'natural' in the strong sense. Deflationists from Carnap to Hirsch deny there is any such fact.

question: Kant's distinction between phenomena (the world as it appears to us) and noumena (things in themselves) has been called incoherent by critics from Jacobi onward. Where does Jacobi's famous attack press?
answer: Kant's system needs noumena as the cause of appearances yet forbids applying causation beyond phenomena — without that prohibited move, no entry into Kant's system can be justified.
choices: Kant's system needs noumena as the cause of appearances yet forbids applying causation beyond phenomena — without that prohibited move, no entry into Kant's system can be justified.
Kant's system needs noumena to ground freedom yet treats freedom as a postulate of practical reason — these two strategies pull in opposite directions and cannot both succeed at once.
Kant's system needs noumena to preserve God's reality yet denies any theoretical knowledge of God — believers can therefore find no genuine comfort in the noumenal placeholder Kant offers them.

Kant's system needs noumena to fix scientific reference yet leaves them in principle unknowable — theoretical physics is thereby cut off from any contact with the underlying realities it would describe.
context: Jacobi's 1787 critique: 'without the thing-in-itself I cannot enter the system, but with it I cannot remain.' Fichte responded by abandoning the noumenon entirely; Schopenhauer reinterpreted it as Will.

question: Kant's third antinomy concerns freedom — the thesis says a free first cause must exist; the antithesis says everything must follow from prior causes. Kant claimed both could be true if applied properly. How does the resolution work?
answer: As phenomenon the agent is part of the causal order and fully determined; as noumenon the agent stands outside time and can be a free first cause — two descriptions, one being, no contradiction.
choices: As phenomenon the agent is part of the causal order and fully determined; as noumenon the agent stands outside time and can be a free first cause — two descriptions, one being, no contradiction.

Free actions occur in special gaps within natural causation, where physical determinism momentarily fails — the human will exploits these openings without violating the otherwise lawful order of nature.
Free choices are uncaused at the start of long causal chains, while ordinary events fall within already-established sequences — freedom and determinism divide the world between distinct event types.
Free agency is a useful fiction the moral life requires, while determinism is the actual truth — Kant grants the appearance of freedom and denies it any genuine ontological reality whatever.
context: Critique of Pure Reason, Third Antinomy resolution; Groundwork III. The 'two-aspects' reading is now standard; the 'two-worlds' reading has nearly disappeared from contemporary scholarship.

question: Spinoza distinguished three kinds of knowledge: imagination (from sense and rumor), reason (from common notions), and a third highest kind he called scientia intuitiva. What does the third kind grasp that the second cannot?
answer: The essence of a particular thing as it follows necessarily from the divine nature — not general laws but the singular reality of this finite being seen in its eternal connection to the whole.
choices: The essence of a particular thing as it follows necessarily from the divine nature — not general laws but the singular reality of this finite being seen in its eternal connection to the whole.
The mystical union of the knower with what is known beyond all conceptual structure — Spinoza absorbed the via negativa of the medieval mystics and placed it above ordinary discursive reasoning.
The future course of particular events from their present causes alone — the third kind functions as a complete predictive science of the kind Laplace would later imagine in its full development.
The personal experience of one's own mental states from the inside — Spinoza placed a privileged first-person introspective faculty at the apex above the publicly accessible faculties of reason.
context: Ethics V, propositions 24–32. The intellectual love of God flows from the third kind of knowledge. Yovel, Della Rocca, and Garrett have all pressed what is left for it to do once reason has shown that everything follows from substance.

question: The Sorites paradox produces a contradiction from accepted premises about heaps. Williamson and Sorensen developed a bold response now called epistemicism. The view sounds paradoxical itself. What does it claim about vague predicates?
answer: Sharp boundaries exist for terms like 'heap' or 'bald' — some precise number marks the line — but the boundaries are unknowable to us, so vagueness is ignorance about a fact, not absence of fact.
choices: Sharp boundaries exist for terms like 'heap' or 'bald' — some precise number marks the line — but the boundaries are unknowable to us, so vagueness is ignorance about a fact, not absence of fact.
Boundaries for vague predicates shift with context and speaker — what counts as a heap in one conversation may not in another, and vagueness reflects this systematic context-dependence.
Vague terms admit degrees of truth between zero and one — three grains has a low truth-value for 'heap,' a thousand has a high one, and standard logic gives way to fuzzy logic in such cases.
Vague terms are simply meaningless in any technical use — ordinary speech tolerates them through pragmatic forgiveness, but no precise reasoning should employ them at any point ever.
context: Williamson's Vagueness (1994), Sorensen's Blindspots (1988). Rivals: degree-theoretic semantics (Goguen, Zadeh), supervaluationism (Fine), contextualism (Raffman). Epistemicism preserves classical logic at the cost of a striking ignorance claim.

question: Aristotle said the goal of a human life is EUDAIMONIA — often translated as 'happiness,' but more like 'flourishing' or 'living well.' Why is this NOT the same as just feeling good?
answer: You can feel good today and still not be living a life worth living over time.
choices: You can feel good today and still not be living a life worth living over time.
Feeling good is illegal under most Greek laws, so it cannot be the goal.
Eudaimonia comes only after death, so feelings during life do not matter.
Aristotle did not believe in feelings, so feeling good cannot be eudaimonia.
context: A drug user can feel good for an hour and live badly for a year. A doctor doing hard work can be tired and exhausted but living an excellent life. Aristotle was after the second kind.

question: When someone responds to an argument by attacking the person making it instead of the argument itself, philosophers call this 'ad hominem' (Latin: 'to the person'). Which case below commits ad hominem?
answer: A senator's healthcare bill is dismissed by listing the senator's past affairs, with the bill's contents never discussed at all in any depth.
choices: A senator's healthcare bill is dismissed by listing the senator's past affairs, with the bill's contents never discussed at all in any depth.
A senator's healthcare bill is dismissed because most senators have voted to support it on the floor of the chamber recently.
A senator's healthcare bill is dismissed because if it passes, the law will lead to a chain of further bills nobody wants.
A senator's healthcare bill is dismissed because the senator changed the original modest claim into a wilder one to mock.
context: Ad hominem swaps the argument for the arguer. A flawed person can still be right; a saint can still be wrong. The argument's truth is independent of who makes it.

question: Appeal to pity (argumentum ad misericordiam) substitutes sympathy for argument. Which case below most clearly commits this move?
answer: 'My defendant's argument for innocence rests entirely on the fact that his elderly mother will be very sad if she has to visit him in prison.'
choices: 'My defendant's argument for innocence rests entirely on the fact that his elderly mother will be very sad if she has to visit him in prison.'
'My defendant's argument for innocence rests on three eyewitnesses who place him in a different city at the time the crime occurred there.'
'My defendant's argument for innocence rests on the camera footage, which shows him in a coffee shop while the burglary was taking place.'
'My defendant's argument for innocence rests on the lack of any physical evidence connecting him to the scene where the crime took place.'
context: Pity matters morally — but it isn't evidence about whether the person did the act. A defendant's family situation has no bearing on what occurred.

question: Denying the antecedent is the second invalid form built from conditionals. Which argument below illustrates denying the antecedent in action?
answer: 'If she trained hard, she'd win. She didn't train hard. So she won't win.' Yet a less-trained gifted athlete could still defeat the others.
choices: 'If she trained hard, she'd win. She didn't train hard. So she won't win.' Yet a less-trained gifted athlete could still defeat the others.
'If she trained hard, she'd win. She trained hard. So she won.' This is straightforward modus ponens applied to a sporting prediction.
'If she trained hard, she'd win. She didn't win. So she didn't train hard.' This is straightforward modus tollens, the valid form here.
'If she trained hard, she'd win. She won. So she trained hard.' This is affirming the consequent, a related but different mistake.
context: The conditional doesn't promise that ONLY hard training wins. Other paths to winning leave the conclusion uncertain even when the antecedent fails.

question: A common mistake: confusing correlation with causation versus the related but distinct post-hoc fallacy. Which case is post hoc rather than mere correlation?
answer: 'I wore my lucky socks Monday and we won. So my socks caused the win.' One event followed another, and causation was inferred from order.
choices: 'I wore my lucky socks Monday and we won. So my socks caused the win.' One event followed another, and causation was inferred from order.
'Towns with more libraries have higher literacy rates.' Two variables co-vary, but no specific event-then-event sequence was asserted.
'Sleep and good grades are positively correlated.' A statistical pattern was reported, with no temporal sequence claimed in the data.
'Coffee consumption tracks productivity across countries.' Two measures rise together, but no event followed another in any one case.
context: Post hoc looks at a specific sequence ('I did X, then Y followed'). Cum hoc (correlation) looks at two things varying together across many cases.

question: Appeals to nature claim something is good (or bad) because it's natural (or unnatural). Why is this generally a fallacy in moral or practical reasoning?
answer: What is natural and what is good come apart in countless cases; smallpox is natural and bad, while medicine is unnatural and good.
choices: What is natural and what is good come apart in countless cases; smallpox is natural and bad, while medicine is unnatural and good.
What is natural and what is good always coincide perfectly; the fallacy is denying the obvious link in cases where it really applies in full.
What is natural and what is good are unrelated questions about words; the fallacy is mistaking a linguistic puzzle for a real moral problem.
What is natural and what is good are the same question; the fallacy is treating them as separate when they are actually one identical issue.
context: Sometimes 'natural' tracks 'good' (a natural diet might suit our biology), but not by itself. The argument has to be made, not assumed by the word.

question: Sometimes apparent fallacies aren't. Citing a relevant expert is legitimate. When does an appeal to authority cross into fallacy territory?
answer: When the cited authority isn't a real expert on the actual question, when experts strongly disagree, or when the appeal substitutes for engaging the evidence.
choices: When the cited authority isn't a real expert on the actual question, when experts strongly disagree, or when the appeal substitutes for engaging the evidence.
When the cited authority happens to disagree with the speaker, the citation becomes hostile and therefore counts as a logical fallacy by definition.
When the cited authority is named rather than anonymous, the citation puts inappropriate weight on a single figure rather than the broader data.
When the cited authority's reputation is well-known, the audience may be biased by name-recognition and so the citation becomes manipulative on that.
context: A cardiologist on heart health: fine. A cardiologist on climate policy: weaker. A famous actor on either: usually irrelevant to the actual question.

question: Anselm: God is that than which no greater can be conceived; existence in reality is greater than in understanding; so God exists. Critics charge Anselm begs the question. Which version of that charge is sharpest?
answer: The premise 'existence is greater than non-existence' assumes existence sits on the perfection-scale at all — what the theist must establish before the argument can run.
choices: The premise 'existence is greater than non-existence' assumes existence sits on the perfection-scale at all — what the theist must establish before the argument can run.
The premise 'God is that than which no greater can be conceived' assumes the concept of God in question, so the conclusion God exists circles on the very definition the argument starts from.
The premise 'we can conceive God' assumes humans have cognitive capacity for the divine, which is itself a theological commitment the argument should leave open and prove, not presuppose.
The premise 'a greater being is conceivable' assumes the maximally great being is unique, which is precisely the property the argument aims to demonstrate rather than to presuppose.
context: Kant: existence isn't a real predicate that adds perfection. A hundred imagined dollars and a hundred real dollars share the same concept; only one has 'reality' which isn't a feature of the concept. The argument trades on a confusion about what existence is.

question: Formal fallacies are mistakes in logical FORM; informal fallacies depend on content, context, or rhetoric. Which is the clearest formal fallacy, and why does the distinction matter?
answer: Affirming the consequent ('if P then Q; Q; so P') is purely formal — invalidity shows without knowing P or Q. Equivocation, ad hominem, and appeal-to-authority are informal and need topic-knowledge.
choices: Affirming the consequent ('if P then Q; Q; so P') is purely formal — invalidity shows without knowing P or Q. Equivocation, ad hominem, and appeal-to-authority are informal and need topic-knowledge.

Ad hominem is the clearest formal fallacy because it has the same structure regardless of topic; the distinction matters because formal fallacies can be cataloged by a single repeating logical pattern.
Equivocation is the clearest formal fallacy because it involves a sliding term breaking logical form across premises; the distinction matters because formal fallacies all involve word-meaning shifts.
Appeal to authority is the clearest formal fallacy because it has a fixed logical shape; the distinction matters because formal fallacies can be evaluated by their citation structure alone.
context: Aristotle's distinction. Formal fallacies are detectable by symbolic analysis (truth tables for propositional; semantic models for predicate). Informal fallacies need topic-knowledge: 'this expert is unreliable HERE' is a content judgment, not a form check.

question: Modal fallacies confuse what is necessarily true with what is true conditionally. Classic: 'Necessarily, if I am thinking, I exist. I am thinking. So I necessarily exist.' What is the precise logical error?
answer: It confuses necessity of the CONDITIONAL ('if-then' is necessary) with necessity of the CONSEQUENT ('I exist' is necessary). Only 'so I exist' is licensed, not 'so I necessarily exist'.
choices: It confuses necessity of the CONDITIONAL ('if-then' is necessary) with necessity of the CONSEQUENT ('I exist' is necessary). Only 'so I exist' is licensed, not 'so I necessarily exist'.
It confuses truth of the antecedent ('I am thinking' is true) with necessity of the antecedent ('I am thinking' is necessary). Only 'so I am thinking' is licensed, not a strengthened modal claim.
It confuses truth of the conditional ('if-then' is true) with truth of the consequent ('I exist' is true). Only 'so the conditional holds' is licensed, not a claim that the consequent follows.
It confuses truth of the consequent ('I exist' is true) with truth of the antecedent ('I am thinking' is true). Only 'so the consequent holds' is licensed, not the move back to the antecedent.
context: In modal logic: from N(P→Q) and P, infer Q, NOT N(Q). The mistake reads 'necessarily, if-then' as 'if-then-necessarily.' Aquinas charged some fatalists with this slip; modern critics charge some defenders of theological foreknowledge with the mirror confusion.

question: Russell's paradox (1902) showed Frege's plausible-looking principle generated a contradiction. Which fallacy did Russell think Frege had committed, and how does the paradox illustrate it?
answer: Unrestricted comprehension: Frege assumed any well-formed property defines a set. The set of all sets not containing themselves both must and must not contain itself, exposing the contradiction.
choices: Unrestricted comprehension: Frege assumed any well-formed property defines a set. The set of all sets not containing themselves both must and must not contain itself, exposing the contradiction.

Begging the question: Frege used the very concept of set to define what counts as a set. The paradox shows the definition circles back on itself in a way that prevents grounding the foundational notion.
Equivocation: Frege used 'set' in two senses, once for collections and once for predicates. The paradox arises because the slide between meanings introduces contradiction when crossing levels.
Category mistake: Frege treated sets as the same logical type as their members. The paradox dissolves once we distinguish levels of the type hierarchy and assign each set its own proper level.
context: The fix was type theory (Russell) or restricted comprehension (ZFC). The paradox killed Frege's logicist project and reshaped 20th-century logic. Russell described receiving Frege's letter: 'I felt that I should have to give up the work of years.'

question: Hume's is/ought gap: moral conclusions can't be derived from purely factual premises. A century later, Moore named a related but distinct error. How are Hume's gap and Moore's naturalistic fallacy related, and how do they differ?
answer: Both target natural-to-normative moves. Hume targets the INFERENTIAL gap (no bridge from 'is' to 'ought'). Moore targets the DEFINITIONAL move (no identifying 'good' with N).
choices: Both target natural-to-normative moves. Hume targets the INFERENTIAL gap (no bridge from 'is' to 'ought'). Moore targets the DEFINITIONAL move (no identifying 'good' with N).
Both target the same problem: Hume identified it as a general ethical challenge; Moore later gave the precise logical formulation. Broad intuition followed by sharpened technical statement.
Both target normative-to-natural moves: Hume said moral terms can't reduce to facts; Moore extended this to biological and evolutionary reductions in late-Victorian moral theory in print.
Both target attempts to define ethical terms: Hume rejected all definitions of moral words; Moore extended the rejection to natural-scientific ones while allowing metaphysical non-natural ones.
context: Hume's gap is about inference (premises to conclusion). Moore's is about identity (the meaning of 'good'). A non-cognitivist can accept Hume's gap while rejecting Moore's open-question argument; a Cornell realist can reject Moore while accepting Hume.

question: Wittgenstein warned against 'philosophical bewitchment' — being misled by surface grammar. He thought many traditional problems were generated by what confusion, and how does this relate to the formal/informal distinction?
answer: Words sharing grammar but no logical form — 'nothing' looks like a name, 'time flows' like a verb-phrase — make philosophers ask 'where does nothing live?' Informal in the deepest sense.
choices: Words sharing grammar but no logical form — 'nothing' looks like a name, 'time flows' like a verb-phrase — make philosophers ask 'where does nothing live?' Informal in the deepest sense.
Words sharing logical form but no grammar — sentences in different surface languages translate into the same structure but grammatical differences mislead philosophers about the underlying logic.
Words sharing a sense but no reference — different terms pick out the same object while looking like different names, prompting philosophers to multiply entities and ask spurious questions.
Words sharing reference but no sense — different terms have different meanings while picking out the same object, prompting philosophers to ask meaning-questions answerable only by reference.
context: Wittgenstein: 'philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language.' Ryle made similar use against 'the ghost in the machine.' Anscombe and Wittgenstein dissolved 'problems' by showing they presupposed conceptual confusions.

question: Begging the question has a precise modern reconstruction beyond syntactic circularity. When does an argument count as question-begging in the technical sense developed by Sinnott-Armstrong and others?
answer: When a premise is supported only by reasons that themselves presuppose the conclusion, so no one not already convinced has any reason to accept the premise — making the argument useless for persuasion.
choices: When a premise is supported only by reasons that themselves presuppose the conclusion, so no one not already convinced has any reason to accept the premise — making the argument useless for persuasion.
When the conclusion is the same sentence as a premise, so the argument moves in a tight syntactic circle detectable by inspection of bare propositional content alone without analysis of reasons.
When it commits a formal logical error in the deductive chain, so the conclusion fails to follow from the premises even though no premise is identical with the conclusion in any stated form.
When its premises rest on testimony from authorities sympathetic to the conclusion, so the evidence chain has been corrupted by selection bias toward witnesses with a stake in the outcome.
context: An argument can be logically valid yet question-begging if its premises are dialectically inert — they fail to give a doubter any reason to move. This is why merely valid arguments don't always persuade, and shouldn't. Validity and persuasive force come apart.

question: Mill in A System of Logic distinguished valid deduction from causal inference. He proposed five methods (agreement, difference, joint, residues, concomitant variation). What fallacy do these methods help us avoid?
answer: Conflation of correlation with causation — especially attributing causation to one of two co-varying factors when both share a hidden third cause. Mill's methods test necessity and sufficiency.
choices: Conflation of correlation with causation — especially attributing causation to one of two co-varying factors when both share a hidden third cause. Mill's methods test necessity and sufficiency.
Conflation of premise with conclusion, especially using a causal claim as its own evidence — Mill's methods test which premises actually support a conclusion versus which restate it in other words.
Conflation of necessity with universality, especially treating universal generalizations as necessary truths — Mill's methods test which generalizations admit exceptions versus which hold uniformly.
Conflation of formal validity with material truth, especially inferring valid conclusions from false premises — Mill's methods test which causal premises are actually true versus merely assumed.
context: Mill's methods were the first systematic empirical approach to causation. They have known limits (modern philosophy of causation distinguishes probabilistic, counterfactual, mechanistic accounts), but post hoc, cum hoc, and confounding-variable mistakes are what Mill attacked.

question: Walton, Krabbe, and the pragma-dialectical school (van Eemeren, Grootendorst) argue classifying a move as 'fallacy' depends on its function in a dialogue, not its abstract form alone. On this approach, what counts as a fallacy?
answer: A move violating rules of reasonable critical discussion — shifting burden of proof, refusing to commit, attacking the person — relative to dialogue type (persuasion, negotiation, inquiry, eristic).
choices: A move violating rules of reasonable critical discussion — shifting burden of proof, refusing to commit, attacking the person — relative to dialogue type (persuasion, negotiation, inquiry, eristic).
A move violating abstract logical form regardless of context — affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent — independent of what conversation is occurring or the parties' goals at the time.
A move violating audience expectations regardless of form — surprising or unfamiliar arguments — independent of whether the move is actually flawed, with novelty itself marking the fallacy.
A move violating the speaker's own prior commitments regardless of context — inconsistency over time — independent of whether the current move is properly evaluated by the discussion's standards.
context: Pragma-dialectics treats argument as a regulated activity aimed at resolving disagreement. Ad hominem in a friendly chat is rude; in a formal debate, it's a procedural violation. The framework lets us see why context matters to whether a move 'is' a fallacy at all.

question: Aristotle's De Sophisticis Elenchis cataloged thirteen fallacies and became the source for medieval and modern lists. Recent scholars (Hamblin, Hansen) have criticized the Aristotelian tradition severely. What's the central critique?
answer: The tradition treats fallacies as items with stable identities recurring unchanged across contexts. Many 'fallacies' are heuristics that mostly work — the binary miscarves the actual phenomenon.
choices: The tradition treats fallacies as items with stable identities recurring unchanged across contexts. Many 'fallacies' are heuristics that mostly work — the binary miscarves the actual phenomenon.

The tradition treats fallacies as universal human errors when they are culturally specific patterns from classical Greek debate practice. Applying the catalog elsewhere imposes alien frameworks on argument.

The tradition treats fallacies as deliberate deceptions when most errors are unintentional cognitive lapses. Calling them 'sophistical' wrongly attributes moral failure where psychology explains them.

The tradition treats fallacies as exclusively formal errors when most everyday failures are content-dependent. The Aristotelian catalog misses the bulk of bad reasoning by focusing on the wrong errors.
context: Hamblin's 1970 Fallacies opened the modern critique: textbooks pass the Aristotelian list around, often with examples that don't fit the definitions. Pragma-dialectical, Bayesian, and virtue-epistemology schools have all proposed reconstructions of the practice.

question: A Bayesian critique of the 'base-rate fallacy' label: what looks like base-rate neglect is sometimes a reasonable response to ambiguous evidence. When does the diagnosis itself become hasty on a sophisticated Bayesian view?
answer: When the base rate comes from a sample of questionable representativeness, or when other relevant information makes the strict prior inapplicable, the diagnosis ignores updating the subject was doing.
choices: When the base rate comes from a sample of questionable representativeness, or when other relevant information makes the strict prior inapplicable, the diagnosis ignores updating the subject was doing.

When the base rate comes from a validated source, the diagnosis stays questionable; subjects departing can always be defended as employing alternative inferential strategies producing different conclusions.

When the base rate is published in a textbook, the diagnosis becomes most reliable; subjects departing have likely failed to read the literature and should be charged with negligence not rationality-failure.

When the base rate is computed by experts, the diagnosis becomes definitive; subjects departing should be charged with technical incompetence in probability calculation rather than a deeper reasoning error.
context: Gigerenzer: heuristics that look 'biased' to a strict Bayesian are often ecologically rational in environments where humans evolved. The base-rate-neglect diagnosis sometimes mistakes a reasonable response to uncertain information for a fixed cognitive bug — charity reveals updating where the textbook saw error.

question: The PRINCIPLE OF CHARITY (Davidson, Quine): read an interlocutor as making the strongest reasonable argument given their evidence. How does charity constrain when accusing someone of strawman is itself a strawman move?
answer: When the accuser caricatures the alleged strawman — treating any summary as willful distortion, ignoring that compression is unavoidable — the accusation fails charity and becomes what it claims to find.
choices: When the accuser caricatures the alleged strawman — treating any summary as willful distortion, ignoring that compression is unavoidable — the accusation fails charity and becomes what it claims to find.

When the accuser identifies a real distortion, charity doesn't require excusing it; the charge stands if the distortion is real, and charity merely requires presenting it accurately. Strawman-of-strawman is rare.

When the accuser fails to use 'strawman' precisely, the accusation becomes invalid; charity requires familiarity with the formal definition before levelling the charge in a serious dialectical exchange.
When the accuser shows the original argument was malformed, the strawman charge is baseless; charity requires the accused's argument to be sound before any distortion could count as strawman at all.
context: Every restatement compresses, and compression always loses something. Calling every compression a 'strawman' weaponizes the term and forecloses paraphrase that genuine dialogue requires. Charitable restatement should be the goal — and graceful correction the response.

question: Appeal to authority is often called a fallacy, but Locke distinguished AD VERECUNDIAM (improper reverence) from legitimate testimony. When does it NOT commit the fallacy on careful contemporary accounts (Goldman, Coady)?
answer: When the expert has relevant expertise, the claim falls in their area, the expert community largely agrees, no conflict of interest distorts testimony, and citation supplements engagement with reasons.
choices: When the expert has relevant expertise, the claim falls in their area, the expert community largely agrees, no conflict of interest distorts testimony, and citation supplements engagement with reasons.

When the expert is widely respected and the citation comes from peer-reviewed publication; under those conditions the appeal becomes immune to challenge and provides decisive grounds for the claim without inquiry.

When the expert holds credentials and uses precise technical vocabulary; under those formal conditions the appeal becomes immune to challenge and provides decisive grounds without inquiry by the audience.

When the expert agrees with the speaker's other commitments and supports their conclusions; under those conditions the appeal becomes immune to challenge and provides decisive grounds without further checks.
context: Coady's Testimony (1992) argued we depend on others' authority for most of what we know. Goldman's social epistemology asks how a non-expert evaluates rival experts. Both reject the strict view that ANY appeal to authority is fallacious — modern life couldn't run that way.

question: Hume's is/ought gap has been challenged by Searle ('How to Derive Ought from Is', 1964) and neo-Aristotelians (Foot, MacIntyre). What's Searle's strategy, and what's the standard reply from defenders of Hume's gap?
answer: Searle: from 'Jones said "I promise to pay $5"' derive 'Jones ought to pay'. Reply: works only because the institution of promising already builds 'ought' into promising, smuggling the bridging premise.
choices: Searle: from 'Jones said "I promise to pay $5"' derive 'Jones ought to pay'. Reply: works only because the institution of promising already builds 'ought' into promising, smuggling the bridging premise.

Searle: from 'humans are social animals' derive 'humans ought to cooperate'. Reply: assumes natural facts about sociality entail normative conclusions — precisely what Hume's gap denies and Searle should overcome.

Searle: from 'valid arguments are truth-preserving' derive 'one ought to argue validly'. Reply: assumes truth-preservation is already a normative goal, smuggling normativity into the supposedly logical premise.

Searle: from 'most punish promise-breakers' derive 'one ought to keep promises'. Reply: assumes punishment patterns track moral truth, requiring bridging premises about the legitimacy of those patterns.
context: Searle runs through 'institutional facts.' Critics charge he just relocates the gap: the institution of promising is itself a normative system, not a bare natural fact. The debate revealed how subtle the 'is' versus 'ought' distinction can become when institutions enter the picture.

question: Genetic fallacy: don't judge a claim by its origin. But virtue-epistemology (Zagzebski) and feminist standpoint theory (Harding) argue origin sometimes IS evidence. How can these positions resist the fallacy?
answer: They distinguish origin OF a belief from reasons supporting it: origin can rationally affect prior probability (tobacco-funded studies warrant scrutiny) without disproving it. Treating origin as sufficient is the fallacy.
choices: They distinguish origin OF a belief from reasons supporting it: origin can rationally affect prior probability (tobacco-funded studies warrant scrutiny) without disproving it. Treating origin as sufficient is the fallacy.

They argue origin is always decisive evidence, so the traditional diagnosis was simply wrong; knowing where a claim came from settles truth-value in most cases, and modern epistemology has corrected the older view.
They argue origin is never decisive and endorse the traditional diagnosis; their work adds that social factors matter besides origin, without challenging that origin alone can't settle truth-value.

They argue origin is decisive only for moral claims, while traditional diagnoses apply to factual ones; this preserves the fallacy for empirical questions while making moral epistemology run by different rules.
context: The mature position: origin is data, not verdict. A claim's history shapes the prior probability we should assign before examining the argument's merits, but it doesn't replace examining them. Calling this 'genetic fallacy' confuses prior-probability-shaping with conclusion-deriving.

question: Some philosophers (Stove, Williamson) argue the formal-fallacy-catalog approach to critical thinking has it backwards: real bad arguments rarely cleanly instance named fallacies. What is the deeper criticism?
answer: Real bad arguments mix errors, exploit ambiguity, lean on shared assumptions; catalog pattern-matching misses actual problems. Better: train evaluative reading, careful definitions, 'what would change my mind.'
choices: Real bad arguments mix errors, exploit ambiguity, lean on shared assumptions; catalog pattern-matching misses actual problems. Better: train evaluative reading, careful definitions, 'what would change my mind.'

Real bad arguments commit only formal errors, but the catalog is incomplete; learning named fallacies misses other formal patterns. Better: extend the catalog systematically until it covers every faulty pattern.

Real bad arguments are detectable only by experts, so catalogs wrongly democratize critical thinking; learning fallacies gives the untrained unjustified confidence. Better: defer to credentialed logicians here.

Real bad arguments are usually deliberate deceptions, so catalogs are too charitable; learning fallacies treats sophists as confused not malicious. Better: train suspicion of motives over structure-analysis.
context: Post-Hamblin tradition. Modern critical-thinking pedagogy increasingly emphasizes virtue-epistemology and dialogical norms (Walton, Tindale) over the pure catalog approach. The catalog remains useful as starting vocabulary; expertise lies in moving beyond it.

question: Wittgenstein-influenced philosophers (Cavell, Anscombe, McDowell) sometimes claim what tradition calls 'fallacies' are often disguised disagreements about meaning. How does this reframing change fallacy-finding?
answer: Fallacies become symptoms of conceptual confusion or disputed schemes rather than discrete errors. Diagnosing 'fallacy' becomes an invitation to clarify what each party means; argument advances by clarification.
choices: Fallacies become symptoms of conceptual confusion or disputed schemes rather than discrete errors. Diagnosing 'fallacy' becomes an invitation to clarify what each party means; argument advances by clarification.

Fallacies are illusions produced by misunderstanding ordinary language and do not exist as a category of genuine reasoning errors. Diagnosing fallacy is a category mistake and should be abandoned as practice.

Fallacies become absolute conceptual errors identifiable by careful linguistic analysis. Diagnosing a fallacy is a decisive refutation that ends discussion rather than continuing it through more clarification.

Fallacies divide into formal logical errors remaining real and informal linguistic ones that dissolve. Diagnosing formal refutes; informal shows confusion. Both kinds remain distinct without further interaction.
context: Cavell on Wittgenstein: philosophical disagreements often turn out to be disagreements about what should count as a relevant consideration. McDowell on disjunctivism: rivals often share 'fallacy' charges that mask a deeper dispute about how to carve up the conceptual terrain at issue.

question: Jeremy Bentham left instructions that his body be dissected, preserved, and displayed at University College London — where it still sits in a glass case. What ethical view did this gesture express?
answer: That the only things with inherent value are pleasure and pain, not bodies or rituals.
choices: That the only things with inherent value are pleasure and pain, not bodies or rituals.
That bodies belong to the state, which may dispose of them however serves the common good.
That the dead can still teach the living, and so corpses should remain near students always.
That immortality is real, and a preserved body keeps the soul anchored to its old home.
context: Bentham called the display his 'auto-icon.' He thought funeral customs were sentimental waste; if a corpse could be useful — for anatomy, for memory, for argument — that was the only question worth asking. The wax-headed figure still gets wheeled into university meetings on rare occasions. The minutes record him as 'present but not voting.'

question: Kierkegaard published most of his major works under invented names like Johannes Climacus and Victor Eremita — not as a hidden author but openly so. Why use the pseudonyms?
answer: Each name held a view he thought worth voicing without claiming as his own conclusion.
choices: Each name held a view he thought worth voicing without claiming as his own conclusion.
He feared arrest by the Danish church and needed the names to confuse the authorities.
He thought philosophical authority required anonymity — true ideas should not bear a face.
He wished to be remembered by all his names and saw fame as the chief aim of writing.
context: Kierkegaard wanted readers to wrestle with positions, not with his biography. Climacus argued one way about Christianity; Eremita compiled the aesthetic Either/Or. The names were transparent in Copenhagen — everyone knew it was him — but they signaled that the views were experiments in a way of life, not the author's settled creed.

question: Schopenhauer thought life was mostly suffering — striving leads to disappointment, satisfaction leads to boredom, then more striving. What did he say offered any relief?
answer: Losing oneself in art, compassion for others, or the silencing of the will the saints practiced.
choices: Losing oneself in art, compassion for others, or the silencing of the will the saints practiced.
Steady civic effort — building institutions that ease the burdens of the next generation along.
Drinking and good company — Schopenhauer recommended convivial Frankfurt life as the cure.
Belief in a benevolent God — only the certainty of heaven could outweigh present suffering.
context: Schopenhauer's pessimism is famous; his escape routes are less so. Aesthetic experience momentarily lifts us out of striving (we contemplate without wanting); compassion recognizes the same Will at work in every sufferer; ascetic denial — Buddhist or Christian — quiets the Will at the source. He thought all three were real, partial reliefs.

question: Adorno and Horkheimer fled Nazi Germany in the 1930s and ended up in Los Angeles — staring at Hollywood film studios. What did they decide mass entertainment was actually doing to its audience?
answer: Producing satisfaction in standard packages that left consumers easier to manage
choices: Producing satisfaction in standard packages that left consumers easier to manage
Reflecting back the genuine creative interests of the working classes that bought tickets
Distracting the public from culture but leaving political judgment essentially untouched
Replacing live theatre with cheaper substitutes but not changing the audience's inner life
context: Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944, written in California exile). The 'Culture Industry' chapter argued that Hollywood, radio, and popular magazines were not democratic culture but industrial production: songs, films, and stars built to a formula, delivering predictable pleasure that trained people to accept what they were given. Adorno and Horkheimer had watched Weimar's politicized public collapse into Nazi spectacle; they saw American mass culture as a softer cousin of the same process.

question: Kuhn noticed something the textbooks hide. Quiet stretches of puzzle-solving are interrupted by sudden upheavals — Copernicus, Newton, Einstein. What did he call these upheavals?
answer: Paradigm shifts — moments when scientists argue about the framework, not just the puzzles.
choices: Paradigm shifts — moments when scientists argue about the framework, not just the puzzles.
Crucial experiments — single tests so decisive they put a long-standing question to rest.
Research programmes — hard cores protected by adjustable auxiliary hypotheses around them.
Anomalous discoveries — surprising results absorbed into existing theory without disruption.
context: Kuhn's 1962 Structure of Scientific Revolutions argued science is not steady accumulation. Normal science works inside a paradigm; revolutions are when the paradigm itself breaks. Lakatos's 'research programmes' is the most serious rival picture.

question: Xenophanes mocked his contemporaries for picturing gods in their own image — Greeks made Greek-looking gods, Thracians red-haired ones. What larger point was he driving at?
answer: That human ideas of the divine reflect the humans more than the divine, and so must be sharply distrusted.
choices: That human ideas of the divine reflect the humans more than the divine, and so must be sharply distrusted.
That the gods of different peoples are real but local, each one ruling only the land where it is worshipped.
That the gods do not exist at all, and stories of them are tools used by rulers to control their subjects.
That the gods, while real, lack any moral character and care nothing about how humans choose to act.
context: Xenophanes drove the point home with a joke: if horses and oxen had hands, he said, they would draw their gods as horses and oxen. He was not quite an atheist — he believed in one supreme deity, unlike anything human — but he was the first systematic critic of religious projection.

question: Anaximenes proposed that everything comes from air — but he gave a specific mechanism his teacher Anaximander had not. How did he say one substance became all the others?
answer: By condensing or thinning: rarefied air becomes fire, thickened it becomes wind, cloud, water, earth, stone.
choices: By condensing or thinning: rarefied air becomes fire, thickened it becomes wind, cloud, water, earth, stone.
By the action of mind on matter: a cosmic intellect imposes form on a passive, formless underlying stuff.
By love drawing things together and strife pulling them apart in repeating cycles across the long ages.
By the constant motion of countless invisible particles whose shape determines what we see and touch.
context: Anaximenes is sometimes treated as the dullest of the Milesians, but he did something his teacher had not: he gave a process. Compression and rarefaction are quantitative changes producing qualitative ones — the seed of every later atomic theory.

question: Tocqueville feared democratic peoples would love equality so deeply they would accept any condition, even servitude, so long as shared. What did he say it did to liberty?
answer: Sap it, since citizens would prefer a level chain to an uneven freedom enjoyed by their neighbors alone.
choices: Sap it, since citizens would prefer a level chain to an uneven freedom enjoyed by their neighbors alone.
Sharpen it, since equal political voice would force rulers to respect each citizen's private freedoms in turn.
Replace it, since the older language of rights would give way to a newer language of welfare and provision.
Reform it, since equal starting conditions alone would let each individual exercise their freedoms in full.
context: Tocqueville thought liberty and equality were both democratic instincts, but unequal partners. Liberty demands effort, courage, and the toleration of difference; equality offers comfort and a kind of moral simplicity. When the two collide, he warned, the comfortable instinct usually wins.

question: Environmental philosophers split: human-centered ethics protects nature because humans need it; nature-centered ethics says nature has its own worth. Bryan Norton noticed something odd: when each camp wrote out actual policies, they kept recommending the same things. He called this the 'convergence hypothesis.' What did he infer?
answer: The intrinsic-value debate has little payoff; long-run human interest protects what nature-first ethics protects.
choices: The intrinsic-value debate has little payoff; long-run human interest protects what nature-first ethics protects.
Only intrinsic-value ethics can justify protection; human reasoning leaves loopholes that pressure exploits.
The camps recommend opposite policies, so environmental philosophy must pick a foundation before advice.
Neither camp justifies policy without religious premises, since secular ethics has no reason to value the unowned.
context: Norton's 1991 Toward Unity Among Environmentalists argued the fight between Rolston-style realists and human-centered pragmatists is largely beside the point: a long-term, multi-generational anthropocentrism converges on the same recommendations. Callicott argued the foundations still matter.

question: Reading other moralists, Hume noticed authors slip without warning from sentences using 'is' to sentences using 'ought.' What did he say this transition demanded?
answer: An explanation: how a new relation, 'ought,' is derived from claims that contain only 'is' is never shown.
choices: An explanation: how a new relation, 'ought,' is derived from claims that contain only 'is' is never shown.
A refutation: the transition is a fallacy and moral claims must be reduced to descriptions of natural facts.
A definition: every 'ought' must be analyzed as shorthand for an 'is' about the speaker's own preferences.
A foundation: morals require revealed law, since reason alone never carries us from world to obligation.
context: In a famous paragraph at the close of Treatise III.i.1, Hume marks the leap from is to ought and asks for an account. He does not say the leap can never be made — only that no writer he has read has shown how. The challenge has driven moral philosophy ever since.

question: Al-Farabi wrote The Virtuous City to complete Plato's Republic — adapted for a world that had received prophetic revelation. What did he say the ideal ruler must be?
answer: A philosopher and a prophet at once — joined to the active intellect so truth reaches him as vivid image.
choices: A philosopher and a prophet at once — joined to the active intellect so truth reaches him as vivid image.
A jurist and a warrior at once — Quranic law in one hand and the sword in the other, defending the city.
A theologian and a king at once — versed in Ash'ari doctrine and ready to enforce orthodoxy on subjects.
A poet and a statesman at once — moving the people through eloquence while administering the laws.
context: Al-Farabi (Alfarabius to the Latins) read Plato's philosopher-king through Aristotle's De Anima and the Quranic prophet. The same truth reaches the rare reasoner through demonstration and the many through imagination; the ideal ruler has both. The result was the first systematic Islamic political philosophy and a major influence on Avicenna and Maimonides.

question: Mill argued political safeguards — votes, courts, elections — could not by themselves secure liberty. A second tyranny remained. What was it?
answer: Tyranny of social opinion — informal pressure to conform that punishes dissent without passing a law.
choices: Tyranny of social opinion — informal pressure to conform that punishes dissent without passing a law.
Tyranny of the educated class — expert consensus that blocks reform faster than electorates can approve it.
Tyranny of the bureaucracy — administrators whose tenure outlasts elections and whose discretion law cannot reach.
Tyranny of inherited wealth — concentrations of capital that distort political choice before any vote is cast.
context: Tocqueville used the phrase first; Mill in On Liberty pressed it past the ballot. Custom, ridicule, and exclusion enforce conformity where statute cannot reach, and the victim has no court of appeal. Mill thought this informal coercion was doing more damage to original character than any law on the books.

question: Montesquieu argued, against pure theorists, that republican government required small states. What was his empirical claim?
answer: Public virtue depends on citizens knowing each other; a vast republic loses the shared mores that sustain free rule.
choices: Public virtue depends on citizens knowing each other; a vast republic loses the shared mores that sustain free rule.
Public credit depends on a single market; a small republic alone can hold the trust that backs its paper money.
Public order depends on a strong executive; a small republic alone can be ruled by one magistrate without abuse.
Public justice depends on a uniform legal code; a small republic alone can be governed by one body of statute.
context: Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws (1748) reasoned from cases — Sparta, Rome, the Italian republics — rather than from first principles. Madison answered him in Federalist 10, arguing that a large republic could remedy the very factions Montesquieu thought small size prevented. The dispute shaped the American founding.

question: Foot late in her career compared the human virtues to the natural properties of plants. She thought the comparison was philosophically substantive, not poetic. What did the comparison establish?
answer: That moral 'good' for a human works the same way as 'good' for an oak — naming what a thing of that kind needs to flourish.
choices: That moral 'good' for a human works the same way as 'good' for an oak — naming what a thing of that kind needs to flourish.
That ethics rests on intuitions of beauty — humans recognize virtue the way they recognize a fine specimen of any natural form.
That morality is reducible to biology — what counts as virtue is whatever evolutionary success in our species has favored historically.
That moral language is metaphorical — talk of human flourishing borrows its sense from plant cases where the term applies literally.
context: Foot's Natural Goodness (2001) re-grounded virtue ethics in species-typical functioning. A defective root system makes for a defective oak; a defective courage or honesty makes for a defective human. The judgment is not arbitrary or sentimental — it picks out what beings of that kind characteristically need to live well.

question: Hughes in The End of Race Politics defended an older civil rights position the contemporary debate had largely abandoned. What did he argue for?
answer: Color blindness — treating individuals according to character and choice, with race as a feature of biography but not the central one.
